newsitem.title: USA: Dow ends above 6,300 for first time, bonds firmer.
newsitem.headline: Dow ends above 6,300 for first time, bonds firmer.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average closed above 6,300 for the first time Thursday as blue-chip stocks set records for the seventh straight session, while bond prices rose on fresh signs of mild inflation.
The dollar tumbled against the Japanese yen amid speculation that the Clinton administration is considering an advocate of a weak dollar for a top job in the White House.

The 30-share Dow average jumped 38.76 points to 6,313, beating Wednesday's record of 6,274.24 and matching the unbroken string of seven consecutive records set in February. The Dow has gained nearly 300 points in the past nine sessions.
The Nasdaq Composite index also set a new high, gaining 9.64 to 1,270.36. The NYSE Composite rose 2.10 to 389.01, a record.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,464 to 970 on active volume of 478 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"We are seeing a significant capitulation of the bearish camp," said Eugene Peroni, chief technical analyst with Janney, Montgomery Scott. "There is a wider gap between the bulls and the bears and a greater urgency to participate as we cross the next century mark."
The market enjoyed more good economic news, which reinforced the view that the economy is slowing from its brisk pace and that inflation remained under control.

The Consumer Price Index rose a moderate 0.3 percent in October after being up an identical amount in September. The data on inflation came one day after the Federal Reserve held interest rates unchanged.
Wall Street also welcomed news that retail sales rose just 0.2 percent in October, which was slightly below Wall Street's forecast of a 0.3 percent rise.

"We got some excellent economic news on CPI and retail sales for the bond market, confirming slow growth and benign inflation and the equity market took its cue from the bond market," said Philip Orlando of Value Line Asset Management.

In the inflation-sensitive bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury rose 13/32, or $4.0625 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to a new eight-month low of 6.42 percent from 6.45 percent on Wednesday.

The dollar rose against the yen after the Journal of Commerce newspaper reported that economist Fred Bergsten, an advocate of a weak dollar, was in line to replace Laura Tyson to head the National Economic Council.
The dollar fell from 111.60 yen to a low of 111.14. It ended at 111.21, below 111.75 late on Wednesday.
The dollar rose to 1.5085 German marks, compared with 1.5077 marks at Wednesday's close.

Copper prices fell on a report that around half a million metric tons of the metal may be stashed in hidden stockpiles. December copper on New York's Commodity Exchange closed 2.05 cents weaker at 95.85 cents a pound.
Heating oil prices rallied as cold weather in the U.S. Midwest and East Coast areas kept stocks tight.

Heating oil for December delivery settled a sharp 2.20 cents higher at 73.40 cents a gallon on the New York Mercantile Exchange. December crude rose 29 cents to $24.41 a barrel and December gasoline added 0.58 cent to 68.92 cents a gallon.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 fell 0.8 points to 3,926.1 and Tokyo's Nikkei 225 average rose 51.60 points to 21,031.04.
